In multi-task reinforcement learning, sharing a policy among various tasks can lead to suboptimal performance or failure when using a common representation. This issue is particularly pronounced in complex, high-dimensional environments with a lot of information, such as in reinforcement learning. When the optimization process tries to reconcile conflicting gradients, it results in interference that can be catastrophic in some cases. This problem has been extensively studied in the context of multi-task supervised and evalution-based RL, but it has not been sufficiently explored in MTL-RL. Our research fills this gap by developing a comprehensive framework that analyzes MTL RL in a Markov decision process using a vast array of policy optimizers and value functions. Our framework allows for fairer comparisons across different studies and provides a structured approach to studying ML methods in RL. Through our framework, we conducted numerical experiments on a simple environment with a model and a complex multi-task setting on the Mountain Car task with a learned model. Our findings show that separating the weight spaces of the policy significantly improves performance in all but the simplest scenarios, which is an innovative approach to increasing robustness in MTL-RL that enhances the stability of model-based optimization. As a result, our proposed modular network architecture enables agents to effectively share a value function while maintaining distinct policy representations.

This article is a discussion of the foundational developments in formal logic that occurred at Chicago University during the years 1933 to 1935. The location was made significant for the advancement of formal logic due to the presence of J. Rosser, a young and dedicated assistant to A. Tarski, who worked in the department of mathematics at Chicago University. We explore the ideas of leading figures in formal logic, including Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and others, and discuss how they shaped the field. In addition, the article examines the technical aspects of axiomatized systems and the limitations they face, as well as the philosophical implications of these limitations. The discussion is contextualized by the historical events of the time, including the impact of World War II on the figures discussed.

This paper seeks to establish the three balls property for functions within the context of Clifford analysis. Building upon a recent achievement by Dyrdkorn in which the three balls property was initially demonstrated for monogenic functions, we aim to prove the three balls property specifically for the Dirac operator. We find that extending the three balls property from monogenic functions to the Dirac operator requires deriving estimates for the growth of polynomial-like functions in this framework. Consequently, a key component of our work involves developing three lemmas that provide growth estimates for these polynomial-like functions.

We propose an innovative approach to infer unknown parameters in inverse problems by combining physics-based simulations with the Counterfactual Generative Adversarial Network (CGAN). Our method ensures that estimated distributions adhere to a target prior distribution, facilitating reliable uncertainty quantification. Through a sequence of adjustments, we enhance the quality of the estimated distributions and reduce bias. Experimental results from image reconstruction tasks validate our approach's effectiveness in utilizing Bayesian inference for Bayesian inference.

This report discusses our findings from the dynamic system fractionally transformed, x(t) = A \cdot x(t), regarding the absence of specific invariant structures such as tori, manifolds, and quadratic surfaces. We specifically examined the conditions under which these invariant structures exist or do not exist, focusing on the relationships between the matrices and vectors involved in the system.

A study of 1155+16's scintillation pattern over a one-year period using the Very Large Array has been conducted to map the distribution of interstellar plasma clouds along the signal's path. By utilizing a semi-analytical scintillation model, detailed maps of plasma density from these clouds have been extracted. This study aims to highlight the limitations of the semi-analytical scintillation model in mapping plasma distributions and presents the statistical properties of plasma distributions as power-law and log-normal probability distributions. These properties are explored in the context of the interstellar medium and plasma streams. Notably, the scintillation model fails to accurately represent the properties of a single large-scale plasma distribution, resulting in biased statistical properties when analyzing interstellar medium properties. As such, the interstellar medium properties should be re-evaluated based on the properties of individual scintillating clouds and their respective populations.

Cross-domain image style transfer transforms an input image to match a target style while retaining its content. To achieve this, we create new unsupervised models that identify target domains which significantly differ from the input, by combining a style encoder with a content encoder in a multi-task framework. These models operate in the feature space and have shown they can transform even extremely noisy or distorted target domains into recognizable ones. We evaluate our approaches on natural images and demonstrate their capability to localize boundaries between input and target domains using only style and content information. Furthermore, we discover that our methods can incorporate additional priors to refine their input-target boundary representations. Experimental results reveal our models' sensitivity to content and their capacity to transform the feature space while maintaining a robust boundary between input and target domains.

The success of graph neural networks in analyzing static graphs can be attributed in part to their ability to pool information from neighboring nodes. To achieve this, many GNN models have adopted Eulerian paths and tree-based structures as a pooling method. However, these approaches are limited when it comes to real-world graphs that contain directed edges with varying weights. As a result, these models may produce inaccurate results in such scenarios. In this work, we introduce a new type of graph neural network called Lorentzian GNN, which is based on a new mathematical structure known as a Fejer convex path. Our model ensures information conservation and utilizes convex combinations to pool information from the graph's nodes as a side benefit. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Lorentxian GNNs through a range of experiments, including link prediction, node classification, and semi-supervised node classification tasks. The results show that our model outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods by significant margins.

A chemical etching process creates patterns on the surface of metallic mirrors used in interferometers, and these designs include both simple shapes and more intricate patterns, but the latter are too complex to effectively describe with basic geometric figures, raising a challenging problem that requires determining the pattern's design in an inverse process, and this in turn can be solved using a computational approach that builds and evaluates different design options through simulations, and this is where a statistical model is used to prioritize and explore the most promising patterns in a high-dimensional design space, and this is in effect similar to inversely solving a partial differential equation to determine the optimal pattern's design.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is linked to the Tsallis parameter. This model, in
its general form, encompasses linear and log-linear impulsivity models as special cases
and allows us to calculate the implisive conversion factor and mean delay. Additionally,
we examine an modified model by considering the mean implisive conversion factor,
which enables the calculation of both the mean delay and the standard deviation.
A comparison between the harmonic and inharmonic gauge choices within the context of the hefty gravity theory is made.

This study translates canonical equilibrium states from the quantum realm to a quasi-probability representation in phase space, specifically the Weyl-Wigner picture. Rather than a singular representation, these states correspond to a superposition of displaced equilibrium states, with their respective phases influenced by external fields and system parameters. Research and numerical simulations reveal that pure states' woven patterns emerge from interactions between periodic system parameters and external variables, whereas canonical states' woven representations involve both such patterns and broader distributions of equilibrium state positions dictated by temperature and system parameters.

The concept of negative absolute temperature has been supported by numerous experiments and theoretical findings, indicating that it represents a legitimate state rather than a paradox. In a substantial number of instances, temperatures below zero have been measured物质ally, although typically relative to references with negative absolute temperatures above zero. However, as demonstrated in both theoretical calculations and actual experiments involving ultracold atoms, such temperatures can exist independently of their environment and be directly associated with a specific physical system. This breakthrough enables the direct application of the notable "negative absolute temperature" formula first derived by Fermi, Tigerstedt, and Tellegen in 1926 to modern contexts, including the description of ultracold atoms.

Within the context of the "scoto-seesaw model," a second-order contribution to the neutrino see-saw mechanism is incorporated via an additional dimension-5 operator, and a second phase see-saw formula is achieved. The "simplest" variant of this model is then proposed by simplifying the operator and phase see-saw parts, specifically using a singlet scalar with one relevant coupling for the operator see-saw and a trivial potential for the phase see-saw. The implications of this model for neutrino mass, the electroweak symmetry breaking, and neutrinoless double beta decay are further explored. In addition, the duration of the inflaton field's evolution and the dark matter phenomenology linked to the singlet scalar are examined, with particular attention to the stability of the Higgs vacuum. Theoretical constraints and phenomenological limits are combined to make a comprehensive set of predictions within this model, with the duration of the inflaton field's evolution and the dark matter mass/decay width ratio emerging as the key parameters. The model's parameters are mapped in detailed plots, with the result that the lower bound for the dark matter decay width being $10^{-29}$ picometers and the lower bound for the dark matter mass being 3.65 times the standard model Higgs boson mass being among the key findings.

Hund's first rule dictates the configuration of electrons in incomplete subshells by favoring upward spin alignment, a rule that holds true in most cases. However, there is an opposing force that influences orbital arrangement known as $\lambda$, which results from the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $t_{1u}$ or $e_g$ and $a_{1g}$ electrons' spin states, requiring the occupation of lower-energy $t_{2g}$ or $e_g$ orbitals for $d^1-d^3$ ion scenarios. We investigate the interaction between $\lambda$ and crystal field splitting in octahedral geometry for 4d and 5d transition metal oxides, specifically those with $M O_3$ compositions, utilizing a spinless tight-binding model. Our findings reveal that $LiCrO_2$ and $NaVO_3$ exhibit $t_{2g}$ - $e_g$ blending, while $NaCrO_2$ and $LiVO_3$ show $e_g$ - $t_{2g}$ blending. These results offer theoretical backing for experimental observations and imply that incorporating $\lambda$ into mean-field and dynamical theories can offer more precise predictions for electron behavior in complex materials.

This paper explores the application of relative Kähler geometry to a relative version of the Hitchin system associated with a smooth projective variety X and a line bundle L over X, along with an integer l. Specifically, we demonstrate that the relative moduli space of stable bundles, denoted as M_X^l, along with an appropriate relative ample line bundle, is itself a relative Frobenius manifold in the sense defined by Lee. Furthermore, if the integer l is sufficiently large, we prove that the total quantum cobrismatiant of M_X^l is isomorphic to the l-th power of the relative quantum cobasismatiant of M_X with the variable rescaled by a factor of 1/l, in the ring of formal power series with rational coefficients in 1/l. These findings are, in part, an extension of the work by Mochizuki.

Images with overlaid illnesses are increasingly used to study and diagnose
medical conditions, though research into images that portray specific conditions
accurately is limited. This is particularly pressing in pediatric medicine where
there's a scarcity of available data, especially for rare and rarest diseases.
Our work explores extending image generation with illness content control for
chest X-rays, building on a baseline that allows generation from seed images
while preserving key features. We integrate multiple generator approaches to
achieve this goal and find the baseline offers the best result fidelity. To
evaluate our methods, we collect a new dataset of around 15,000 images linked to
both child names and detailed medical reports from clinical visits. Our analysis
reveals that latent variables are only partially interpretable and suggests
linear activation manipulation as a more effective tool for controlled generation.
Though not fully automatic, this approach generates images of specific conditions
on original images with high fidelity, as evidenced by lower FID scores and
acceptable quality preservation scores. Our code and models are available online.

ViDaExpert is an application designed for multidimensional data visualization and analysis, including textual content. It enables users to interactively manipulate various components of their datasets through the use of linear and nonlinear visualization techniques such as PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP. Key features include user-defined node weighting, dimension scaling, and multiple visualization methods for network, scatter plot, and scatter-slink diagrams. ViDaExpert is capable of processing large datasets with up to a million rows and provides a plugin for the ViTa viewer application to export export vis.
